title: Systems of Equations
bigQuestion: When two rules are both true at once, how do you find the one pair of numbers that satisfies them both?

story.title: When Does the Tortoise Get Caught?
story.kicker: An old fable becomes a math problem the moment you draw both runners on the same graph.
paragraphs: Everyone knows the fable: the tortoise and the hare agree to race, the hare is far faster, and the hare loses anyway by stopping for a nap. Ms. Okafor's class in Chicago decided to make the story into numbers. They gave the tortoise a head start of 300 meters and a steady speed of 1 meter per second. They gave the hare a speed of 5 meters per second, starting from the line. The question was simple. If the hare never naps, when does it catch the tortoise?

The class drew a graph with seconds along the bottom and meters from the starting line up the side. The tortoise's line began at 300 and climbed gently, 1 meter for each second. The hare's line began at 0 and climbed steeply, 5 meters for each second. Two lines, two rules. Each line by itself told where one runner was at any moment. The interesting spot was where the lines crossed.

At the crossing, both runners are the same distance from the line at the same time. That is the catch. The students read the point off the graph: about 75 seconds, about 375 meters. Then they checked with the equations. Tortoise: 300 + 1 × 75 = 375. Hare: 5 × 75 = 375. Both rules gave the same number, so the crossing was exact. The hare catches the tortoise 75 seconds into the race, 375 meters down the track.

Then someone added the nap. Suppose the hare stops at 60 seconds and sleeps for 100 seconds. The hare's line goes flat at 300 meters from second 60 to second 160, while the tortoise's line keeps climbing. At second 160 the tortoise is at 300 + 160 = 460 meters, far ahead. Now there is a new crossing to find, and a new question: does the hare still catch up before the finish?

A pair of rules that must both be true at once is called a system of equations. Its solution is the point where the graphs meet. This chapter shows how to find that point by graphing, by substitution and by elimination, how to tell when there is no such point or many of them, and how to use systems for phone plans, tickets and coins.
story.think: Without the nap, the hare catches the tortoise at 75 seconds. If the tortoise's head start were doubled to 600 meters, would the catch happen at double the time? Work it out and explain.

lessons.title: What a System Is
lessons.mainIdea: A system of equations is two equations that must both be true, and its solution is the one pair (x, y) that works in both.
reading: Two numbers add up to 10, and their difference is 4. Call the larger number x and the smaller y. The first sentence says x + y = 10. The second says x − y = 4. Together the two equations form a *system of equations*. Many pairs fit the first equation alone: (5, 5), (8, 2), (9, 1). Many fit the second alone: (6, 2), (8, 4), (10, 6). The *solution of a system* is a pair that fits both at the same time.

Test (8, 2). First equation: 8 + 2 = 10, true. Second: 8 − 2 = 6, not 4. So (8, 2) is not a solution. Test (7, 3). First: 7 + 3 = 10, true. Second: 7 − 3 = 4, true. Both equations are satisfied, so (7, 3) is the solution. The two numbers are 7 and 3.

On a graph, each equation is a line, and every point on that line makes its equation true. The solution of the system is the point where the two lines cross, because that is the only point on both lines. For x + y = 10 and x − y = 4, the lines cross at (7, 3). There is no other point on both lines, so there is no other solution.

To check a proposed solution, substitute it into both equations, not just one. Take y = x − 4 and y = 2x − 9 with the point (5, 1). First: 5 − 4 = 1, true. Second: 2 × 5 − 9 = 10 − 9 = 1, true. So (5, 1) is a solution. A point that passes one equation and fails the other is not a solution. Both checks must pass.

words.d: two or more equations that must all be true at the same time
a pair of values (x, y) that makes every equation in the system true

look.title: Sum 15, Difference 3
look.text: Two numbers have a sum of 15 and a difference of 3. With x the larger and y the smaller: x + y = 15 and x − y = 3. Try (9, 6). Sum: 9 + 6 = 15, true. Difference: 9 − 6 = 3, true. So (9, 6) is the solution. Try (10, 5): the sum is 15, but the difference is 5, so it fails the second equation.
look.prompt: Two numbers have a sum of 20 and a difference of 8. Write the two equations, find the pair that works in both, and show both checks.

check.q: Is (7, 3) a solution of the system x + y = 10 and x − y = 4?
choices: It fits only the first equation
check.why: Substitute into both: 7 + 3 = 10 is true and 7 − 3 = 4 is true. Both pass, so (7, 3) is the solution.

check.q: What is the solution of a system of two equations?
choices: a pair (x, y) that makes both equations true
the y-intercept of the first line
the slope of the second line
check.why: A solution must satisfy every equation in the system. On a graph, that is the point where the lines cross.

check.q: Is (5, 1) a solution of y = x − 4 and y = 2x − 9?
choices: No, it fails the second equation
No, it fails the first equation
There is no way to tell
check.why: First: 5 − 4 = 1. Second: 2 × 5 − 9 = 1. Both equal the y-value 1, so (5, 1) satisfies both.

lessons.title: Solving by Graphing
lessons.mainIdea: Graph both lines on one grid; the point where they cross is the solution, and substituting checks it.
reading: Solve the system y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7 by graphing. Graph the first line: start at (0, 1) and use slope 2 to reach (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7). Graph the second: start at (0, 7) and use slope −1 to reach (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4). The point (2, 5) is on both lists. That is the *intersection*, where the two lines cross, so the solution is (2, 5).

Always check the *point of intersection* in both equations. First: 2 × 2 + 1 = 5. Second: −2 + 7 = 5. Both give 5, so (2, 5) is exact. If a check fails, either the graph was drawn wrong or the crossing was read wrong. Redraw with care and look again.

Try y = x + 3 and y = 3x − 1. First line: (0, 3), (1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6). Second line: (0, −1), (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 8). They share (2, 5). Check: 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 × 2 − 1 = 5. Notice that the second line starts lower but climbs faster, so it catches the first, just like the hare catching the tortoise.

Graphing is quick and it shows the picture, but it has limits. It works best when the crossing lands on a *lattice point* with whole-number coordinates. If the lines cross at something like (1.4, 5.2), reading it off a grid gives only an estimate. The next lesson deals with that. Also watch for careless slopes: one line drawn with the wrong slope will cross in the wrong place, and the check will catch it.

words.d: the place where two lines cross
the (x, y) coordinates of the crossing point; the solution of the system
a point on a grid whose coordinates are both whole numbers

look.title: Two Lines, One Crossing
look.text: Graph y = x + 3 and y = 3x − 1 on the same grid. The first passes through (0, 3), (1, 4), (2, 5) and (3, 6). The second passes through (0, −1), (1, 2), (2, 5) and (3, 8). Both lists contain (2, 5), so the lines cross there. Check: 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 × 2 − 1 = 5.
look.prompt: Graph y = 2x and y = −x + 6 on grid paper. Where do they cross? Substitute the crossing point into both equations to prove it.

check.q: Where do the lines y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7 cross?
check.why: At x = 2, the first gives 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 and the second gives −2 + 7 = 5. Both lines pass through (2, 5).

check.q: Where do the lines y = x + 3 and y = 3x − 1 cross?
check.why: At x = 2, y = 2 + 3 = 5 and y = 3 × 2 − 1 = 5. The point (1, 4) is on the first line only, since 3 × 1 − 1 = 2.

check.q: Solving by graphing works best when ___.
choices: the crossing point has whole-number coordinates
check.why: A crossing at a lattice point can be read exactly from the grid. Fraction coordinates can only be estimated from a graph.

lessons.title: Estimating and Checking
lessons.mainIdea: When the crossing is not on a grid corner, estimate it from the graph, then use algebra to find the exact point and check it.
reading: Graph y = 3x + 1 and y = −2x + 8. The first line rises steeply from (0, 1). The second falls from (0, 8). They cross somewhere between x = 1 and x = 2, a little above y = 5. From the picture, a reasonable *estimate* is (1.5, 5). But is that exact? *Check by substitution*: 3 × 1.5 + 1 = 5.5, and −2 × 1.5 + 8 = 5. The two equations give different values, so (1.5, 5) is close but not the true crossing.

To get the exact point, set the two expressions for y equal, since y is the same at the crossing: 3x + 1 = −2x + 8. Add 2x to both sides: 5x + 1 = 8. Subtract 1: 5x = 7. Divide: x = 7/5 = 1.4. Then y = 3 × 1.4 + 1 = 4.2 + 1 = 5.2. Check in the second equation: −2 × 1.4 + 8 = −2.8 + 8 = 5.2. Both agree, so the exact solution is (1.4, 5.2).

The estimate was not wasted. It told us the answer should be near x = 1.5 and y = 5, so the algebra result of (1.4, 5.2) makes sense. If the algebra had given (14, 52), the graph would show that something went wrong. Use the graph to predict the size of the answer, and use algebra to nail it down.

Two mistakes are common here. One is trusting a graph reading as exact just because it looks right. Always substitute into both equations. The other is checking only one equation. The point (2, 5) fits y = 2x + 1 perfectly, but for y = −x + 6 it gives −2 + 6 = 4, not 5. A point must pass both checks to be a solution.

words.d: a careful guess that is close to the exact value, like reading a point from a graph
put the x and y values into each equation and see whether both sides come out equal

look.title: Close, but Is It Exact?
look.text: Graph y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 6. The first rises from (0, 1) through (1, 3) and (2, 5). The second falls from (0, 6) through (1, 5) and (2, 4). The lines cross between x = 1 and x = 2, near y = 4.5. The point (2, 5) is a tempting guess, but in the second equation −2 + 6 = 4, not 5. Setting 2x + 1 = −x + 6 gives 3x = 5, so x = 5/3, about 1.67, and y is about 4.33.
look.prompt: Use the graph to estimate the crossing of y = x + 1 and y = −2x + 6. Then set the expressions equal, solve for x, and compare your exact answer to your estimate.

check.q: A student estimates (1.5, 5) for the crossing of y = 3x + 1 and y = −2x + 8. What does substitution show?
choices: The equations give 5.5 and 5, so the estimate is close but not exact
The first gives 5 and the second gives 5.5
check.why: 3 × 1.5 + 1 = 5.5 and −2 × 1.5 + 8 = 5. Different values mean (1.5, 5) is not on both lines.

check.q: What is the exact solution of y = 3x + 1 and y = −2x + 8?
check.why: 3x + 1 = −2x + 8 gives 5x = 7, so x = 1.4. Then y = 3 × 1.4 + 1 = 5.2, and −2 × 1.4 + 8 = 5.2 confirms it.

check.q: Why should you check a point you read from a graph?
choices: Graph readings can be off by a little; substitution shows whether the point is exact
To find the slope of the line
Checking is not needed if the graph is neat
check.why: A pencil line and a grid can only show so much. Substituting into both equations proves whether the point truly fits.

lessons.title: Substitution
lessons.mainIdea: When one equation gives a variable by itself, substitute that expression into the other equation and solve.
reading: Solve y = 2x − 3 and 3x + y = 12. The first equation already has y by itself: y equals 2x − 3. So wherever y appears in the second equation, put 2x − 3 in its place. This is *substitution*. The second equation becomes 3x + (2x − 3) = 12. Combine: 5x − 3 = 12. Add 3: 5x = 15. Divide: x = 3. Then go back to the first equation: y = 2 × 3 − 3 = 3. The solution is (3, 3). Check: 3 × 3 + 3 = 12, true.

Substitution also works when x is the variable alone. Solve x = y + 4 and 2x + 3y = 23. Replace x in the second equation with (y + 4): 2(y + 4) + 3y = 23. Distribute the 2: 2y + 8 + 3y = 23. Combine: 5y + 8 = 23. Subtract 8: 5y = 15, so y = 3. Then x = 3 + 4 = 7. Check: 2 × 7 + 3 × 3 = 14 + 9 = 23, true. The solution is (7, 3).

If neither equation has a variable alone, *isolate* one first. In x + y = 20 and y = 3x, the second already gives y. Substitute: x + 3x = 20, so 4x = 20 and x = 5. Then y = 3 × 5 = 15. Check the first: 5 + 15 = 20. The solution is (5, 15). Substitution is the natural choice whenever one equation starts with y = or x =.

The most common error is forgetting the parentheses. In 2x + 3y = 23 with x = y + 4, writing 2y + 4 + 3y instead of 2(y + 4) + 3y loses the 8 and gives the wrong answer. Put the whole expression in parentheses, then distribute. Another error is stopping after finding x. A solution is a pair, so find y too, and check the pair in the equation you did not use to find it.

words.d: replacing a variable with an expression that equals it, so an equation has only one variable left
to get a variable alone on one side of an equation, like y = 3x

look.title: One Variable at a Time
look.text: Solve y = x + 1 and 4x + y = 21. The first equation gives y, so replace y in the second: 4x + (x + 1) = 21. Combine: 5x + 1 = 21. Subtract 1: 5x = 20. Divide: x = 4. Then y = 4 + 1 = 5. Check in the second equation: 4 × 4 + 5 = 21, true. The solution is (4, 5).
look.prompt: Solve y = 2x and x + y = 18 by substitution. Show the equation with only x in it, solve it, find y, and check your pair in both equations.

check.q: Solve y = 2x − 3 and 3x + y = 12. What is x?
Solve x = y + 4 and 2x + 3y = 23. What is y?
check.why: 2(y + 4) + 3y = 23 gives 2y + 8 + 3y = 23, so 5y = 15 and y = 3. Then x = 7.

check.q: Solve y = 3x and x + y = 20. What is the solution?
check.why: x + 3x = 20 gives 4x = 20, so x = 5 and y = 3 × 5 = 15. The pair (15, 5) has x and y switched.

lessons.title: Elimination by Adding
lessons.mainIdea: When a variable has opposite coefficients in the two equations, add the equations to eliminate it.
reading: Solve x + y = 12 and x − y = 2. Look at the y terms: +y in the first and −y in the second. They are opposites. Add the two equations, left side to left side and right side to right side: (x + y) + (x − y) = 12 + 2. The y terms cancel, leaving 2x = 14, so x = 7. Put x = 7 into the first equation: 7 + y = 12, so y = 5. The solution is (7, 5). Check the second: 7 − 5 = 2, true. This method is *elimination*.

Adding works whenever a variable's *coefficients* are opposites. Solve 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 2y = 0. The y coefficients are +2 and −2. Add: 8x = 16, so x = 2. Then 3 × 2 + 2y = 16, so 6 + 2y = 16, 2y = 10, y = 5. Check the second: 5 × 2 − 2 × 5 = 10 − 10 = 0, true. The solution is (2, 5).

When the coefficients are the same instead of opposite, subtract one equation from the other. Solve 4x + y = 14 and 2x + y = 8. Both have +y. Subtract the second from the first: (4x − 2x) + (y − y) = 14 − 8, which is 2x = 6, so x = 3. Then 2 × 3 + y = 8 gives y = 2. Check the first: 4 × 3 + 2 = 14, true. The solution is (3, 2).

Two slips to avoid. First, adding the left sides but not the right sides: if you add x + y and x − y, you must also add 12 and 2. Second, subtracting carelessly when the signs are already opposite. With +y and −y, subtracting would give 2y, not 0, and nothing is eliminated. Choose add when the signs differ and subtract when they match.

words.d: adding or subtracting two equations so that one variable cancels out
the number in front of a variable; in 5x − 2y, the coefficients are 5 and −2

look.title: Cancel and Solve
look.text: Solve 2x + y = 11 and 3x − y = 9. The y coefficients are +1 and −1, opposites, so add the equations: 5x = 20, which gives x = 4. Substitute into the first: 2 × 4 + y = 11, so y = 3. Check the second: 3 × 4 − 3 = 12 − 3 = 9, true. The solution is (4, 3).
look.prompt: Solve x + y = 9 and x − y = 1 by adding. Then solve 5x + y = 17 and 2x + y = 8 by subtracting. Check each answer in both equations.

check.q: Solve x + y = 12 and x − y = 2 by elimination.
check.why: Adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7. Then 7 + y = 12 gives y = 5. Check: 7 − 5 = 2.

check.q: Solve 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 2y = 0. What is x?
check.why: Adding eliminates y: 8x = 16, so x = 2. Then y = 5, and 5 × 2 − 2 × 5 = 0 checks.

check.q: For 4x + y = 14 and 2x + y = 8, why subtract the equations instead of adding?
choices: Because the y coefficients are opposites
Because the x coefficients are the same
Because the y coefficients are the same, so subtracting removes y
check.why: Both equations have +y. Subtracting gives y − y = 0, which eliminates y and leaves 2x = 6.

lessons.title: Elimination With Multiplying
lessons.mainIdea: If no coefficients match, multiply one or both equations by a number so that a variable's coefficients become equal or opposite, then eliminate.
reading: Solve 2x + 3y = 12 and x + y = 5. No coefficients match yet. But if you *multiply through* the second equation by −2, it becomes −2x − 2y = −10, and now the x coefficients are +2 and −2. Add: (2x − 2x) + (3y − 2y) = 12 − 10, so y = 2. Then x + 2 = 5, so x = 3. Check the first equation: 2 × 3 + 3 × 2 = 6 + 6 = 12, true. The solution is (3, 2).

Multiplying an equation by a number keeps it true, as long as you multiply every term, including the number on the right. That is why the method works. Sometimes both equations need multiplying. Solve 3x + 2y = 7 and 2x + 5y = 12. To eliminate x, make both x coefficients 6, the *least common multiple* of 3 and 2. Multiply the first by 2: 6x + 4y = 14. Multiply the second by 3: 6x + 15y = 36.

Now subtract the first new equation from the second: (6x − 6x) + (15y − 4y) = 36 − 14, so 11y = 22 and y = 2. Substitute into 3x + 2y = 7: 3x + 4 = 7, so 3x = 3 and x = 1. Check the other original equation: 2 × 1 + 5 × 2 = 2 + 10 = 12, true. The solution is (1, 2).

The usual mistake is multiplying only the left side. If 2x + y = 7 becomes 4x + 2y = 7 instead of 4x + 2y = 14, everything after is wrong. Multiply every term. Also, choose which variable to eliminate by looking for the smaller multiplier. In 2x + y = 7 and 3x + 2y = 12, doubling the first equation to 4x + 2y = 14 lines up the y terms right away, and subtracting the second gives x = 2, then y = 3.

words.d: to multiply every term on both sides of an equation by the same number
the smallest number that two numbers both divide into; for 3 and 2 it is 6

look.title: Line Up the Terms
look.text: Solve 2x + y = 7 and 3x + 2y = 12. Multiply the first equation by 2 to get 4x + 2y = 14. Now both equations have 2y. Subtract the second from the new first: (4x − 3x) + (2y − 2y) = 14 − 12, so x = 2. Then 2 × 2 + y = 7 gives y = 3. Check the second original equation: 3 × 2 + 2 × 3 = 6 + 6 = 12, true.
look.prompt: Solve 3x + y = 10 and 2x + 3y = 9. Decide which equation to multiply and by what, eliminate one variable, and check your solution in both original equations.

check.q: Solve 2x + 3y = 12 and x + y = 5.
check.why: Multiply the second by −2: −2x − 2y = −10. Add to the first: y = 2. Then x = 3. Check: 2 × 3 + 3 × 2 = 12 and 3 + 2 = 5.

check.q: To eliminate x from 3x + 2y = 7 and 2x + 5y = 12, you multiply the first by 2 and the second by 3. Why those numbers?
choices: Because 6 is the least common multiple of 3 and 2, so both x coefficients become 6
Because then the y terms cancel
check.why: 3 × 2 = 6 and 2 × 3 = 6. With equal x coefficients, subtracting the equations removes x.

check.q: Solve 3x + 2y = 7 and 2x + 5y = 12. What is y?
check.why: 6x + 4y = 14 and 6x + 15y = 36. Subtract: 11y = 22, so y = 2. Then 3x + 4 = 7 gives x = 1.

lessons.title: One, None, or Infinitely Many
lessons.mainIdea: Two lines can cross once, never cross, or be the same line, giving one solution, no solution, or infinitely many.
reading: Most systems have exactly one solution, because two lines with different slopes cross exactly once. But two other things can happen. Take y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 4. Both have slope 2, so they are *parallel lines*: they run side by side and never meet. There is no point on both lines, so the system has no solution.

Algebra says the same thing. Set the expressions equal: 2x + 1 = 2x − 4. Subtract 2x from both sides: 1 = −4. That is false no matter what x is. A false statement with the variables gone means no solution. Compare that with y = 3x + 2 and 2y = 6x + 4. Divide the second by 2: y = 3x + 2. It is the very same line. Set them equal: 3x + 2 = 3x + 2, which gives 2 = 2, true for every x.

When both variables disappear and what is left is true, the two equations describe one line, and every point on it is a solution. That is *infinitely many solutions*. So there are three cases. Different slopes: one solution. Same slope, different y-intercepts: no solution. Same slope and same y-intercept: infinitely many.

Do not confuse the false case with a solution of 0. If substitution leads to 0 = 7, the answer is not x = 0 or x = 7. It means the lines never meet. And do not read 0 = 0 as no solution. It means the opposite, that every point on the line works. Say the words out loud: 0 = 7 is false, so no solution; 0 = 0 is true, so infinitely many.

words.d: lines with the same slope that never cross
what a system has when both equations describe the same line, so every point on it works

look.title: Sort the Systems
look.text: System 1: y = 4x + 3 and y = 4x − 2. System 2: y = x + 5 and y = −x + 5. System 3: y = 2x − 6 and 3y = 6x − 18. In System 1 the slopes match but the intercepts differ, so the lines are parallel and there is no solution. In System 2 the slopes differ, so there is one solution, at (0, 5). In System 3, dividing the second equation by 3 gives y = 2x − 6, the same line, so there are infinitely many solutions.
look.prompt: Write your own system with no solution and another with infinitely many. Then explain how a student could tell them apart without graphing.

check.q: How many solutions does the system y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 4 have?
choices: no solution, because the lines are parallel
check.why: Both lines have slope 2 but different y-intercepts, so they never cross. Setting them equal gives 1 = −4, which is false.

check.q: How many solutions does the system y = 3x + 2 and 2y = 6x + 4 have?
choices: infinitely many, because they are the same line
check.why: Dividing 2y = 6x + 4 by 2 gives y = 3x + 2, the first equation. Every point on that line satisfies both.

check.q: Substitution in a system leads to the statement 0 = 7. What does that mean?
choices: The system has infinitely many solutions
check.why: 0 = 7 is false for every value of x, so no pair (x, y) can satisfy both equations. The lines are parallel.

lessons.title: Reading the Count From Slopes
lessons.mainIdea: Rearrange both equations into y = mx + b and compare: different m means one solution, same m with different b means none, same m and b means infinitely many.
reading: Equations do not always arrive in *slope-intercept form*. Solve 2x + y = 6 and 4x + 2y = 8 for y. *Rearrange* the first: y = −2x + 6. Rearrange the second: 2y = −4x + 8, so y = −2x + 4. Both have slope −2, but the y-intercepts are 6 and 4. Same slope, different intercept: parallel lines, no solution.

Now x − y = 1 and 3x − 3y = 3. From the first: −y = −x + 1, so y = x − 1. From the second: −3y = −3x + 3, so y = x − 1. Same slope and same intercept. The two lines *coincide*, meaning they lie exactly on top of each other. Infinitely many solutions: any point on y = x − 1, such as (1, 0) or (5, 4).

One more: y = 5x + 1 and y = −x + 7. The slopes are 5 and −1, different, so there is exactly one solution. Find it: 5x + 1 = −x + 7, so 6x = 6, x = 1, and y = 5 × 1 + 1 = 6. Check the second: −1 + 7 = 6, true. Whenever slopes differ, the lines must cross somewhere, even if the crossing is far off the page.

The trap is comparing equations before rearranging them. The pair 2x + y = 6 and 4x + 2y = 8 does not look parallel, because the coefficients are different. But every term in the second is double the first, except the 8, which would need to be 12. Rearranging shows the shared slope. The other trap is comparing only slopes and forgetting intercepts. Same slope tells you parallel or identical; the intercept decides which.

words.d: an equation written as y = mx + b, so the slope m and y-intercept b can be read directly
to move terms in an equation so it has a different form, like solving for y
to lie exactly on top of one another; two coinciding lines are really one line

look.title: Rearrange, Then Compare
look.text: Take x + 2y = 8 and 3x + 6y = 12. Solve each for y. First: 2y = −x + 8, so y = −(1/2)x + 4. Second: 6y = −3x + 12, so y = −(1/2)x + 2. Both slopes are −1/2, but the intercepts are 4 and 2. The lines are parallel, and the system has no solution. If the second equation had been 3x + 6y = 24, it would have rearranged to y = −(1/2)x + 4, the same line, and there would be infinitely many solutions.
look.prompt: Rearrange 2x + y = 5 and 6x + 3y = 15 into slope-intercept form. How many solutions does the system have? Change one number to give it exactly one solution.

check.q: How many solutions does 2x + y = 6 and 4x + 2y = 8 have?
check.why: Rearranged, the lines are y = −2x + 6 and y = −2x + 4. Same slope, different intercepts, so they are parallel.

check.q: How many solutions does x − y = 1 and 3x − 3y = 3 have?
check.why: Both rearrange to y = x − 1. The lines coincide, so every point on the line is a solution.

check.q: Which system has exactly one solution?
check.why: Only the last pair has different slopes, 5 and −1. The first two pairs are parallel, and the third pair is the same line.

lessons.title: Two Phone Plans
lessons.mainIdea: When two plans have different fixed costs and different rates, the system's solution is the break-even point where they cost the same.
reading: Plan A costs $25 a month plus $2 for each gigabyte of data. Plan B costs $10 a month plus $5 per gigabyte. Each plan has a *fixed cost*, the part you pay no matter what, and a rate. Let g be the gigabytes and c the cost. Plan A: c = 2g + 25. Plan B: c = 5g + 10. Which plan is cheaper depends on how much data you use.

Find where the plans cost the same. Set the costs equal: 2g + 25 = 5g + 10. Subtract 2g: 25 = 3g + 10. Subtract 10: 15 = 3g, so g = 5. At 5 GB, Plan A costs 2 × 5 + 25 = 35 and Plan B costs 5 × 5 + 10 = 35. That point, (5, 35), is the *break-even point*. Below 5 GB, Plan B is cheaper because its fixed cost is lower. Above 5 GB, Plan A is cheaper because its rate is lower.

Test it. At 2 GB: A is 4 + 25 = 29, B is 10 + 10 = 20, so B wins by $9. At 8 GB: A is 16 + 25 = 41, B is 40 + 10 = 50, so A wins by $9. On a graph, Plan B starts lower but climbs faster, and it crosses above Plan A at 5 GB. The steeper line always ends up on top eventually.

The setup is where mistakes happen. The number that multiplies g is the per-gigabyte rate, and the number added alone is the fixed cost. Writing c = 25g + 2 for Plan A would mean $25 per gigabyte, which is a very different plan. Read the words carefully: per means it multiplies, and a month means it is added once.

words.d: the part of a price you pay no matter how much you use; the y-intercept of a cost line
the point where two costs are equal; the solution of the system of cost equations

look.title: Two Plans Side by Side
look.cite: Example plans made for this lesson: A is $25 plus $2 per GB, B is $10 plus $5 per GB
look.prompt: At which amount of data do the plans cost the same? Which plan would you pick if you use 3 GB a month, and which for 12 GB? Explain using the rates.

check.q: Plan A is c = 2g + 25 and Plan B is c = 5g + 10. Where do they cost the same?
At 8 GB, which plan is cheaper, and by how much?
check.why: A: 2 × 8 + 25 = 41. B: 5 × 8 + 10 = 50. A is cheaper by 50 − 41 = 9 dollars.

check.q: Plan A is $25 a month plus $2 per GB, and Plan B is $10 a month plus $5 per GB. Which system matches?
check.why: The per-GB rate multiplies g, and the monthly fee is added once. So A is 2g + 25 and B is 5g + 10.

lessons.title: Tickets, Coins and Mixtures
lessons.mainIdea: Many word problems give a count and a total; write one equation for each, then solve the system.
reading: A school play sells adult tickets for $8 and child tickets for $5. One night 30 tickets sold for $195 in all. How many of each? Let a be the adult tickets and c the child tickets. The count gives one equation: a + c = 30. The money gives the other: 8a + 5c = 195. This is a *mixture problem*: two kinds of things are mixed, and you know the total count and the total value.

Solve by elimination. Multiply the count equation by 5: 5a + 5c = 150. Subtract it from the money equation: (8a − 5a) + (5c − 5c) = 195 − 150, so 3a = 45 and a = 15. Then c = 30 − 15 = 15. Check the money: 8 × 15 + 5 × 15 = 120 + 75 = 195, true. Fifteen adult tickets and fifteen child tickets.

Coins work the same way. A jar holds 20 coins, all dimes and quarters, worth $3.05. Work in cents to avoid decimals: d + q = 20 and 10d + 25q = 305. Multiply the first by 10: 10d + 10q = 200. Subtract from the second: 15q = 105, so q = 7. Then d = 20 − 7 = 13. Check: 10 × 13 + 25 × 7 = 130 + 175 = 305 cents, which is $3.05. Seven quarters and thirteen dimes.

To *set up* any problem of this kind, ask two questions. What is being counted, and what is the total count? What is each one worth, and what is the total value? The first answer gives the count equation with plain variables. The second gives the value equation with each variable multiplied by its worth. The common slip is putting the total value into the count equation, like d + q = 305. The count of coins is 20, and the value in cents is 305. Keep them in separate equations.

words.d: a problem with two kinds of items where you know the total count and the total value
to translate a word problem into equations before solving

look.title: Nickels and Dimes
look.text: A pocket has 25 coins, all nickels and dimes, worth $1.85. In cents: n + d = 25 and 5n + 10d = 185. Multiply the first by 5: 5n + 5d = 125. Subtract from the second: 5d = 60, so d = 12. Then n = 25 − 12 = 13. Check: 5 × 13 + 10 × 12 = 65 + 120 = 185 cents. Thirteen nickels and twelve dimes.
look.prompt: A jar has 18 coins, nickels and quarters, worth $2.50. Write the two equations in cents, solve the system, and check that your coins add up to both the count and the value.

check.q: Adult tickets are $8 and child tickets are $5. Thirty tickets sold for $195. How many adult tickets were sold?
check.why: a + c = 30 and 8a + 5c = 195. Multiply the first by 5 and subtract: 3a = 45, so a = 15. Check: 8 × 15 + 5 × 15 = 195.

check.q: A jar has 20 dimes and quarters worth $3.05. How many quarters are there?
check.why: d + q = 20 and 10d + 25q = 305. Subtracting 10 times the first gives 15q = 105, so q = 7. There are 13 dimes.

check.q: Which pair of equations fits: 25 coins, nickels and dimes, worth $1.85?
check.why: The count of coins is 25, so n + d = 25. Each nickel is 5 cents and each dime 10 cents, and the total is 185 cents.

review.q: Where do the lines y = x + 2 and y = 2x − 1 cross?
review.why: x + 2 = 2x − 1 gives x = 3, and y = 3 + 2 = 5. Check: 2 × 3 − 1 = 5.

review.q: Solve x + y = 9 and x − y = 1.
review.why: Adding gives 2x = 10, so x = 5. Then y = 9 − 5 = 4. Check: 5 − 4 = 1.

review.q: How many solutions does y = 4x + 3 and y = 4x − 2 have?
review.why: Same slope 4, different intercepts 3 and −2. The lines are parallel and never cross.

review.q: Solve y = x + 5 and 2x + y = 17 by substitution.
The tortoise has a 300 m head start and moves 1 m/s. The hare moves 5 m/s. When does the hare catch up?
review.why: 300 + t = 5t gives 300 = 4t, so t = 75 seconds. Both are then at 375 meters.
Subtracting the second from the first gives 2y = 6, so y = 3. Then 2x + 3 = 7 gives x = 2. Check: 4 + 9 = 13.

review.q: The point (1, 4) satisfies y = 3x + 1 but gives 1 + 2 = 3, not 4, in y = x + 2. So (1, 4) is ___.
choices: not a solution of the system
a solution of the second equation only
review.why: A solution must satisfy both equations. Failing one equation means it is not a solution of the system.

review.q: Plan A is c = 2g + 25 and Plan B is c = 5g + 10. At 2 GB, which is cheaper?
review.why: A: 2 × 2 + 25 = 29. B: 5 × 2 + 10 = 20. Plan B is cheaper at 2 GB.
